interviewQuestions.question: How would you design the sync mechanism for a note-taking app, including how you'd detect and resolve conflicts?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use delta sync once the dataset is large enough to matter — each note carries a version number or last-modified timestamp, and the client tracks a sync cursor so it can ask the server 'what's changed since I last synced' instead of re-downloading everything. For a small dataset, full sync is simpler and genuinely fine; I wouldn't add delta sync's complexity before profiling shows it's actually needed.

For detecting conflicts, I'd lean on version numbers over plain timestamps where possible — they're immune to clock skew and directly signal 'this record changed since the version I last saw,' which is enough to detect a conflict even without capturing full causality. Vector clocks would be overkill here unless the product specifically needs to distinguish true concurrent edits from causally-ordered ones.

For resolution, I'd differentiate by field: if two devices changed different fields of the same note (title vs. body) while both offline, I'd merge both changes rather than picking one — that requires tracking changes at field granularity, not just 'this note changed.' If the same field was genuinely edited concurrently — the body text itself, on two devices — I'd either surface it to the user directly ('this note was edited on two devices, keep mine / keep theirs / view both') or, for a product investing more heavily in this, use a text CRDT that merges character-level edits automatically.

The sync loop itself pushes local changes first, then pulls remote changes, so the server has this device's latest state before this device asks what else changed — avoiding a spurious conflict against data this device was about to overwrite anyway.

**Testing:** whether you can design the concrete pieces — detection, resolution strategy per data type, sync ordering — rather than describing 'sync' abstractly.

interviewQuestions.question: Users occasionally report that likes or comment counts on posts seem inflated after a period of poor connectivity. How would you investigate and what's your leading hypothesis?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My leading hypothesis is a missing or broken idempotency key on the sync/write path — an inflated count after poor connectivity is the textbook symptom of a retried write being applied twice, because the client sent the increment, the server processed it, the confirmation was lost on the flaky connection, and the client's retry logic sent the same increment again with no way for the server to recognize it as a duplicate.

I'd confirm by checking the actual write path for that increment operation: does each queued write carry a stable, unique key (ideally the client-generated change ID, not something regenerated per attempt), and does the server-side handler check for and reject a request bearing a key it's already processed, rather than blindly applying the increment again? If the key is missing entirely, or if it's regenerated on each retry attempt rather than reused, that's the bug.

I'd also check whether this correlates specifically with poor connectivity in the actual telemetry (retry counts, timeout logs) rather than assuming — a genuinely different bug (a double-tap on the like button not being debounced, for instance) could produce a superficially similar symptom, and I wouldn't want to ship an idempotency fix for a bug that's actually somewhere else.

Once confirmed, the fix is adding (or fixing) the idempotency key on the write and deduplication on the server, plus a targeted test that specifically simulates a lost-confirmation-then-retry scenario, since that's exactly the condition a clean-network test suite wouldn't naturally exercise.

**Testing:** whether you connect a vague symptom ('counts seem inflated') to the specific mechanism (idempotency) and know how to actually verify it rather than guess.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between last-write-wins and a CRDT-based approach for resolving conflicts, and when would you choose each for a collaborative to-do list app?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
LWW resolves a conflict by discarding one side outright — whichever change has the later timestamp (or version) wins, and the other is gone with no trace, no merge attempt. It's simple and cheap, and it's the right choice for data where a lost edit genuinely doesn't matter — a 'last opened' timestamp, a UI preference synced across devices.

A CRDT is structurally different: it's a data type designed so concurrent updates always merge into a well-defined result with no decision needed, because the merge logic is baked into the structure's own math rather than being a policy choice applied after the fact. For a to-do list specifically, a set-based CRDT can let two devices independently add or remove items while offline and merge cleanly on reconnect — adds from both devices show up, and a delete only removes what was actually deleted, without one device's changes clobbering the other's the way LWW applied to the whole list would.

I'd choose LWW for fields where the product genuinely doesn't care about a rare lost edit, and I'd reach for a CRDT specifically for the parts of this to-do list where concurrent edits from multiple devices or multiple collaborators are a real, expected part of usage — which for a genuinely collaborative to-do list, is probably the item list itself, not metadata like 'last synced at.'

The trade-off I'd flag explicitly: CRDTs add real complexity to the data model and aren't a good fit for every data shape, so I wouldn't reach for one by default — only where the conflict rate and the cost of a lost edit both justify it.

**Testing:** whether you understand these as genuinely different mechanisms with different trade-offs, not just 'LWW is basic, CRDT is advanced, use the advanced one.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Your team is building a note app and initially chose last-write-wins for the note body 'because it's simple.' Six months later, users start complaining about lost edits. How do you approach the migration to a better strategy without a full rewrite?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't try to retrofit CRDT-level sophistication across the whole sync system at once — that's a large, risky change to make under active complaint pressure. I'd first quantify the actual problem: how often are true concurrent edits to the same note actually happening in production (probably rare for most users, more common for a specific subset — heavy multi-device users, or shared notes if that's a feature), since that tells me whether this needs a system-wide fix or a targeted one.

If concurrent edits are rare but costly when they happen, the cheapest real improvement is detecting the conflict rather than silently resolving it — track a version number per note, and when a sync would overwrite a note whose server version has changed since this device last saw it, don't apply LWW silently; instead, keep both versions locally and surface a lightweight 'this note changed elsewhere too — view both?' prompt. That's a meaningfully smaller change than introducing a text CRDT, and it directly fixes the actual user complaint (silent data loss) without needing to redesign the underlying data model.

If the product genuinely needs true concurrent multi-device editing as a core feature going forward (not just an edge case to stop losing data on), that's the point where I'd propose the larger investment — a CRDT-based text model — as a deliberate roadmap item, not a reactive patch, since that's a real multi-sprint undertaking that deserves its own planning rather than being rushed in response to a complaint spike.

**Testing:** whether you can propose a proportionate, incremental fix instead of jumping straight to the most sophisticated solution regardless of actual need.
